subject: How to change the correlation structure of the latent variables in lavaan (syntax) ?

messages.author: b430763ad49e6cd0
messages.subject: How to change the correlation structure of the latent variables in lavaan (syntax) ?
parts:
Hi, 

I am doing a longitudinal CFA study with 4 time points. 
After establishing strong measurement invariance (equal factor loadings over time, and equal indicator intercepts over time), I am conducting tests to simplify the correlation / covariance structure among the latent constructs. 

A first structure I tested was compound symmetry, which implies the variance and covariance are constant over the four time points. This is a rather strong assumption, and my chi-square test "failed" (p = 0.002). 
I defined the syntax of the latent constructs / variables as follows:

# Equal covariance and variance of the latent construct over time
Time0 ~~ CV*Time1 + CV*Time3 + CV*Time4
Time1 ~~ CV*Time3 + CV*Time4
Time3 ~~ CV*Time4

Time0 ~~ VAR*Time0
Time1 ~~ VAR*Time1
Time3 ~~ VAR*Time3
Time4 ~~ VAR*Time4

I now want to test another structure: autoregressive. This implies a constant variance over time, and a decreasing correlation over time. As for the correlation: between time 0 and 1 the correlation = rho, between time 1 and 2 the correlation = rho, but between time 0 and 3 the correlation is rho^2 (or: rho * rho). For simplicity: I am assuming equidistant times here. 

How can I do this in Lavaan? I tried: CV*CV*Time and CV^2*Time, but these are unknown operations in lavaan. 

Thanks for helping me out. 

Kind regards, 
Amonet

You do this with constraints.

Something like:

Time0 ~~ CV01*Time1 + CV03*Time3 + CV04*Time4
Time1 ~~ CV13*Time3 + CV14*Time4
Time3 ~~ CV34*Time4
 
# constraints
CV01 == CV13
CV01 == CV34

CV03 == CV01^2
CV34 == CV01^2  

etc.

(These models can be more sensitive to starting values, so if you get convergence problems, try that.)

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: How to change the correlation structure of the latent variables in lavaan (syntax) ?
parts:
You do this with constraints.  Something like:

Time0 ~~ CV01*Time1 + CV03*Time3 + CV04*Time4
Time1 ~~ CV13*Time3 + CV14*Time4
Time3 ~~ CV34*Time4
 
# constraints
CV01 == CV13
CV01 == CV34

CV03 == CV01^2
CV34 == CV01^2

The constraints idea is a good one, but autoregressive structure does not apply the power to the covariance but to the correlation.  So the covariance between Time 1 and 2 (or any adjacent times) would be $\sigma^2 \times \rho$ and the covariance between Time 1 and 3 (or any times twice as far apart) would be $\sigma^2 \times \rho^2$

I would add 2 things to Jeremy's advice:
  • First test whether the latent variances are the same, since simple autoregressive structure implies constant variance over time. If you use a marker variable (std.lv = FALSE), you constrain latent variances to equality and compare to the measurement-invariance model.  If you identify the model by fixing the variance at one occasion to 1, then you test the same hypothesis by fixing all latent variances to 1 and comparing to the measurement-invariance model.  These are equivalent models, so either way, if you cannot reject the null hypothesis that latent variances are similar over time, then you should use std.lv = TRUE so that the latent covariance estimates are actually latent correlations (which are what you actually want to apply those constraints to).
  • If you cannot reject the null about homogeneous latent variances, then you should not bother testing the more restrictive autoregressive structure.  Instead, you can test heterogeneous autoregressive structure (see Table 41.5 here, or chapter 7 in Singer & Willett's Applied Longitudinal Data Analysis), which allows variance to change over time.  Phantom constructs can be used to estimate a statistically equivalent model to the measurement-invariance model, but allow you to estimate latent correlations instead of covariances.  The trick is described in Todd Little's Longitudinal SEM book if you have it.  Basically, for each construct whose variance is not already fixed to 1, you specify that it loads onto a higher-order construct whose variance is fixed to 1.  For the model to be identified, you fix the lower-order (original) factor to have a variance of zero, and freely estimate the "factor loading" on the higher-order phantom construct.  For example:
Time0ph =~   Time0
Time0ph ~~ 1*Time0ph
Time0   ~~ 0*Time0

The free factor loading is therefore the latent SD (square-root of the previously estimated latent variance).  For this to work, you only estimate latent correlations among the phantoms (and any first-order factors whose variances are already fixed to 1).  You fix to zero all latent covariances among the lower-order factors that have phantom constructs, as well as covariances between those lower-order factors and any phantoms.  The resulting model should have the same df and test statistic as the measurement-invariance model; if not, then the specification is incorrect.

Once that is done, then you can add the constraints that Jeremy recommended (i.e., label the correlation estimates, and constrain all first-orders to have the same value, and for higher-orders to be raised to the power of how many occasions apart they are).

Regarding starting values, I would look at the less-constrained model in each model comparison as a guide (e.g., pick a first-order correlation starting value that is somewhere in the middle of the freely estimated ones).  
 
Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

Thanks a lot for your elaborate advice. I have Todd D. Little's book :) it's been very useful throughout this study (and so has been all your advice here and on SEMNET ;) )
I managed to get the syntax correctly thanks to you both. 

Is it correct that I specify the latent means through the original parameterisation? That is: Time0 ~ 1, and not: Time0ph ~ 1. So, I left the phantom constructs' intercepts unspecified, and had the 'normal constructs' as it was before (latent means estimated). I'd like to know this because I want to test if the latent means are equivalent over time, after having 'agreed' on / found a satisfying / simpler correlation structure for the latent constructs. 

P.s. for those who are interested, the syntax is as follows - based on the advice given by Jeremy and Terrence:

# equal latent variances (or stdev) over time (ph = phantom construct): 
Time0ph =~ V*Time0
Time1ph =~ V*Time1
Time3ph =~ V*Time3
Time4ph =~ V*Time4

# AR(1) correlation structure
Time0ph ~~ CV01*Time1ph + CV03*Time3ph + CV04*Time4ph
Time1ph ~~ CV13*Time3ph + CV14*Time4ph
Time3ph ~~ CV34*Time4ph 

# constraints as suggested by Jeremy:

CV01 == CV13
CV01 == CV34

CV03 == CV01^2

CV14 == CV03
CV04 == CV01^3

Kind regards,
Amonet

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: How to change the correlation structure of the latent variables in lavaan (syntax) ?
parts: Is it correct that I specify the latent means through the original parameterisation? That is: Time0 ~ 1, and not: Time0ph ~ 1.

Yes, although the models estimating the mean of Time0ph v. Time0 would be statistically equivalent, yielding the same model-implied observe means.  The issue is interpretation.  Estimating the latent mean of Time0ph would be a standardized mean (i.e., Cohen's d), equivalent to the estimate of Time0~1 divided by Time0ph=~Time0 (i.e., the SD of Time0) if you were to estimate Time0~1 instead.  To the degree that latent SDs change over time, testing standardized v. unstandardized means could be quite different.  Because the scale of the construct is arbitrary, it might be arbitrary which latent means you want to test for equivalence (standardized or unstandardized means), so just be clear which test you are reporting.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: How to change the correlation structure of the latent variables in lavaan (syntax) ?
parts: Not sure if I am mixing things up, but I am using the effects coding method that is used throughout the book of Little as well.

The idea is the same, but Little is showing you how to use effects coding on the intercepts among indicators of the same construct to identify (and estimate) that construct's mean.  I was saying you could apply effects coding to the latent means across occasions to identify (and estimate) all of them.  There is nothing stopping you from doing both, but neither one requires the other.
I understood that this scale isn't arbitrary, since I don't arbitrarily pick one of the manifest variables to be the scale of the latent construct.

Well, if that is what makes it non-arbitrary, then fixing the means to zero is also non-arbitrary.  I think his description is misleading because effects coding is still arbitrary in the sense that you can constrain the estimates so that their average is any arbitrary value (just like you could fix the latent means to any value besides zero to identify them).  

What makes ALL of these identification methods arbitrary is that common factors have no scale of measurement.  Having a location/scale of measurement requires actually measuring the variable.  We don't measure the common factor, we only measure the indicators that we believe are directly effected by the common factor, so the indicators have a scale of measurement, but the common factors do not.  And no identification method gets around that fact -- they are all ways of making sure there is a unique solution, conditional on arbitrary identification choices.
Does this mean testing the unstandardized means might make more sense?

I'm not sure it matters.  If you were testing observed variables, I would say test them both, because it would be interesting to test whether actual means or standardized means (Cohen's d) are equivalent.  But since the metric is arbitrary, technically it is possible to identify the model such that the estimated means ARE standardized.  

Sorry to be so noncommittal, but it really seems arbitrary. If the latent variances change very little over time, then the tests should lead to the same conclusions either way.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen
